title: The one who would not bow
hook: every angel bows to Adam except Iblis, who says he was made of fire and is better (7:11–12)
tomorrow: The garden and the one tree

segments.voice: Yesterday: the names God taught Adam, and the angels who said, we know only what we were taught. Your line was to name is to notice. What did you learn the name of? Day twenty-four.
screen: `THE NAMES — TO NAME IS TO NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Someone new joins the team, younger, less experienced, and the boss says: they're leading this one. For some people, something goes tight in the chest. Me? Under them? Nobody says it out loud. Some wouldn't even admit it to themselves. But the thought can arrive fully formed: I'm better than that. Today's story turns on that exact thought. It doesn't begin with a crime or a lie. It begins with a comparison. A whole company of heavenly beings is told to bow to Adam. They all do. All but one.
screen: `SOMEONE NEW IS PUT IN CHARGE.` → `I'M BETTER THAN THAT.` → `ALL BOW BUT ONE.`

segments.voice: The scene is told several times in the Qur'an. God tells the angels to bow before Adam, and they fall down, all of them, except Iblis. God asks him what kept him from bowing when he was told. And Iblis answers, in Pickthall's words: “I am better than him. Thou createdst me of fire while him Thou didst create of mud.” Notice his argument. It isn't about God at all. It's about material. Fire rises and shines; mud just sits there. So I'm better. It's a snob's logic, and it's the whole of his argument. Commentators point out what he left out: the names, the knowledge, the breath God blew into Adam. He looked at the clay and stopped there. Who was Iblis? One verse says plainly that he was of the jinn, beings made of smokeless fire. Scholars differ: some say he was a jinn who'd risen to live among the angels; others that he was an angel himself. And the name? Some link it to an Arabic root for despair; others say it comes from outside Arabic. And the bow? Scholars explain it as a bow of honor to Adam, not worship, which in Islam is only for God. Islamic teaching takes pride seriously. A hadith in Muslim's collection says no one with a speck of pride in their heart will enter paradise, and then defines it: pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people. That's Iblis exactly. Not a monster, at first. Just someone who said: I'm better than him.
screen: `ALL BOWED, EXCEPT IBLIS.` · `FIRE IS BETTER THAN MUD.` · `JINN OR ANGEL? SCHOLARS DIFFER.` · `PRIDE: REFUSING TRUTH, SCORNING PEOPLE.` · then, large: `I AM BETTER THAN HIM.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Think back over the last day or two. Look for one moment when the thought appeared: I'm better than them. Smarter. Kinder. More careful. Better dressed. It might have been about a stranger, a coworker, a family member. Don't scold yourself. Just find it and look at it, the way you'd look at a stone in your shoe. Then think of one thing that person has that you don't. If you pray, you can ask for help to see it. The bell holds the time.
Iblis. The one who would not bow to Adam, because he thought fire was better than mud.
Your line: pride was the first mistake. Today, notice one moment of I'm better than, and in that moment, find one thing to admire in the other person. Day twenty-four.

screen: `DAY 24 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GARDEN AND THE ONE TREE.`

howItsDone: Muslims learn this story as a warning against pride, and many recall it when they bow in prayer: the bow Iblis refused is the bow they choose, five times a day, to God.

original.note: Arabic: the name of the one who would not bow. some link it to a root for despair; others say it comes from outside Arabic.

trapdoor: what you thought: the devil, a monster from the start.
what it means: Iblis — the one who refused to bow to Adam, because he judged himself better by what he was made of.

what a scholar hears: 18:50 calls him one of the jinn; scholars differ on jinn or angel; the name may come from b-l-s, despair, or from outside Arabic; pride defined in Muslim's collection as refusing truth and scorning people.

sources.quoted: I am better than him. Thou createdst me of fire while him Thou didst create of mud.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 91 (pride: rejecting truth and looking down on people)
Qur'an 55:15 (the jinn created of smokeless fire)

notes: Pickthall 7:12 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording ('...(Iblis) said: I am better than him. Thou createdst me of fire while him Thou didst create of mud.').
Jinn or angel: the script presents both views (e.g. al-Hasan al-Basri held he was never an angel; others, via Ibn 'Abbas, that he was among the angels). Confirm.

Etymology of Iblis: from ablasa (to despair) per some Arab philologists; many (including al-Tabari's discussion) treat it as non-Arabic, often linked to Greek diabolos. The script doesn't name Greek. Confirm.
Bow of honor (sujud tahiyya) vs worship: the standard explanation. Confirm.
'The breath God blew into Adam' refers to 15:29 / 38:72. Confirm.
Muslim 91 cited from memory ('an atom's/mustard seed's weight of pride'); paraphrased as 'a speck'. Confirm.
